Mark the student's response to a question from the 2025 NSW HSC Modern History exam strictly against the official marking criteria, exactly as an HSC marker would: award marks only for what is actually written, do not be generous, and quote the criteria row the response fits. Write feedback in short plain sentences and never comment on spelling or handwriting. Judge the response the way HSC Modern History markers do: a direct answer to the question, a sustained judgement where the directive verb asks for one, specific and accurate evidence (dates, names, cases, legislation, sources, historians) and the terms of the course. Do not reward length or narrative for its own sake.

Question 10 (a) [25 marks]: Bolshevik ideology was successfully implemented through the economic policies of the Soviet Union between 1917 and 1941. Evaluate the accuracy of this statement.

MARKING CRITERIA (out of 25):
21–25 marks: Provides a sophisticated and sustained judgement which demonstrates an extensive understanding of the issue(s) raised in the question | Supports the argument with extensive and accurate historical knowledge and understanding including specific evidence and interpretation | Communicates through a well-structured, logical and cohesive response using a wide range of relevant historical terms and concepts appropriately
16–20 marks: Provides a reasoned and sustained judgement which demonstrates a sound understanding of the issue(s) raised in the question | Uses a range of relevant and accurate historical information which may include interpretation to support the judgement | Communicates through a structured and logical response using a range of relevant historical terms and concepts
11–15 marks: Provides a judgement which demonstrates some understanding of the issue(s) raised in the question | Presents a range of accurate historical information in the context of the question | Communicates through a structured response using some relevant historical terms and concepts
6–10 marks: Describes and/or narrates a range of historical information in the context of the question | Communicates some relevant historical terms and concepts
1–5 marks: Provides some relevant historical information


ANSWERS COULD INCLUDE (the student does not need every point):
The various economic policies of the Soviet Union throughout the period 1917 to 1941 did not all align with Bolshevik ideological principles. At times, economic policy required ideological compromise for the sake of maintaining power. Stalin’s economic policies, while addressing some elements of Bolshevik ideology such as collective ownership and a planned economy, also made significant reinterpretation of Marxist-Leninist principles.
Key points could include:
• The New Economic Policy: allowed a return of capitalist elements in the economy, encouraging peasants’ opportunity to increase their wealth and small-scale trade within the cities. The NEP abandoned the restrictive measures of war communism, which had introduced a command economy and lost considerable support from among the workers and peasants.
• Debate over modernisation: Competing visions for the USSR, given Russia’s lack of capitalist development, required major ideological revision leading Bolshevik figures.
Some such as Bukharin saw the NEP as a long-term vehicle to build capitalism in Russia, before a truly communist society could be established. Others on the Left, such as Trotsky believed the NEP was a temporary measure to restore the economy which had been devastated after the Civil War. Once Stalin rose to power, he set about ending the NEP, arguing that it had created new class enemies which contradicted the notion of a classless society.
• Forced collectivisation: While Stalin could claim that the policy of collectivisation fulfilled the ideological principle of shared ownership, the methods by which this was implemented against a reluctant peasantry betrayed Lenin’s concept of a smychka, or alliance between peasant and worker. Furthermore, the prioritisation of grain exports to raise capital led to widespread famine, abandoning the Bolshevik principle of ‘from each according to their ability’ to ‘each according to their need’.
• Five-year plans: The greatest betrayal of Bolshevism was the repression of the industrial working class under the five-year plans. All remains of worker solidarity, workplace rights, and collective decision-making were abandoned for the sake of production targets.
